title: Choosing the right material: grip for a tray, slip for a slide

summary.text: Put a steel katori on a tilted plastic sheet, and it slides off. Put it on rubber, and it stays, even when the board is steep. A material is right for a job when it has the properties the job needs. Your child tests five materials as a mat for a tray, and measures how high the board can go before the katori slides. Then they use the same results to choose a material for a slide, where the winner is the other way round.
summary.art: A child lifting one end of a chopping board covered with rubber bands, with a steel katori sitting still on it, and a ruler standing upright at the lifted end.

intro.hook: Put a steel tumbler on a steel plate. Tilt the plate more and more. Now put a rubber band round the tumbler's bottom and try again. What changes?
intro.text: Without the rubber band, the tumbler slides. With the rubber band, it stays on until the plate is much steeper. The tumbler is the same. Only the material it stands on is different. Every job needs a material with the right properties. A tray of tumblers needs grip. A slide in the park needs the opposite. Before you read on, guess. Which material in your home grips best?
intro.art: A child's hand tilting a steel plate, with one steel tumbler sliding off and another, with a rubber band round its base, staying put.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a job needs, and choose a material that has those properties.
By the end I can test which material grips a katori best, by tilting a board and measuring how high it goes.
By the end I can say what friction is: the grip between two things that touch.
By the end I can explain why the same property can be right for one job and wrong for another.
By the end I can tell which properties a job needs, and which it does not need.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of. Rubber, steel, cotton, paper and plastic are materials.
terms.example: A chappal sole is made of rubber. A katori is made of steel.
terms.art: A rubber chappal, a steel katori and a cotton hanky, each with a label for its material.

terms.meaning: What a material is like, or what it does. Waterproof, bendy, hard and grippy are properties.
terms.example: Rubber is bendy and grippy. Steel is hard and shiny.
terms.art: A rubber band being bent and a steel spoon that stays straight, with the words 'bendy' and 'hard'.

terms.meaning: Right for a job, because it has the properties the job needs.
terms.example: Rubber is suitable for a chappal sole. Paper is not, because it tears when wet.
terms.art: A rubber chappal with a green tick, and a paper chappal falling apart in a puddle with a red cross.

terms.meaning: The grip between two things that touch. Friction stops things sliding.
terms.example: Friction between your chappal and the road stops you slipping.
terms.art: A close-up of a chappal sole pressing on a road, with small arrows showing the grip.

terms.meaning: Has very little friction, so things slide on it easily.
terms.example: A wet bathroom floor and a polished steel slide are slippery.
terms.art: A child sliding down a shiny steel slide in a park.

terms.meaning: Stiff. It does not bend easily.
terms.example: A steel plate and a wooden chopping board are rigid.
terms.art: Two hands trying to bend a wooden chopping board, which stays straight.

terms.example: A rubber band, a hanky and a plastic bag are flexible.
terms.art: A hanky being folded and a rubber band being bent into a curve.

terms.meaning: A test where only one thing changes, so you know what made the difference.
terms.example: In the tilt test, only the material changes. The katori, the coins and the board stay the same.
terms.art: The same katori with coins shown on five boards, each covered with a different material.

explanations.concept: Choosing a material: start with the job
explanations.context: This card explains how to choose a material for something you want to make.
explanations.definition: A material is suitable for a job when it has the properties the job needs. Properties the job does not need do not matter.
explanations.description: First ask what the job needs. A tumbler must hold water and not break when it is dropped. Steel does both, so steel is suitable. Steel is also shiny, but a tumbler does not need to be shiny. A raincoat must keep water out and bend when you move. Plastic does both. Steel keeps water out too, but a steel raincoat could not bend.
examples: A towel must soak up water, so it is made of cotton.
A window must let you see through it and keep the rain out, so it is made of glass.
A tray mat must stop tumblers sliding, so rubber is a good choice.
explanations.art: A steel tumbler with two labels: 'holds water, does not break' in green, and 'shiny' crossed out in grey.

explanations.concept: Friction: why rubber grips and plastic slips
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the tilt test: why the katori stayed on the rubber long after it slid off the other materials.
explanations.definition: Friction is the grip between two things that touch. More friction means a thing needs a steeper slope, or a harder push, before it slides.
explanations.description: Every surface has tiny bumps, too small to see. Even a shiny katori has them. Rubber is soft, so it squashes into the bumps under the katori and touches it in many more places. More touching means more grip. A hard, smooth plastic sheet touches the katori in fewer places, so the katori slides off sooner.
examples: Chappal soles, bicycle handle grips and the feet of a mixie are rubber, for grip.
A slide in the park is smooth steel or plastic, so children slide down.
Wet tiles are slippery, because a thin layer of water keeps your feet from touching the tiles.
explanations.art: A zoom-in picture: soft rubber squashing into the tiny bumps under a steel katori, and beside it a hard plastic sheet touching the katori only at a few bump tops.

explanations.concept: Cloth bag or plastic bag: more than one thing to think about
explanations.context: This card is about a choice many families make at the vegetable shop. People who think carefully still disagree about it.
explanations.description: We also ask what a material costs, how long it lasts, and what happens to it when it is thrown away. A thin plastic bag is cheap and light, but it can stay as litter for a very long time. Making one cloth bag uses much more water and energy than making one plastic bag. But a cloth bag lasts for years. So a cloth bag is the kinder choice only if you use it many, many times.
examples: A cotton or jute bag used every week for years.
A thin plastic bag used once and thrown away.
An old plastic bag used again and again until it tears.

perspectives.explanation: Plastic bags are cheap and keep wet vegetables from leaking. Customers want them.

perspectives.who: A volunteer who cleans a beach in Chennai
perspectives.explanation: We pick up plastic bags from the sand every week. Cloth bags would mean less litter.

perspectives.who: Scientists who add up everything a bag uses
perspectives.explanation: A cloth bag must be used many times before it does less harm than a plastic bag. The best bag is the one you already have, used for as long as it lasts.

explanations.art: A girl at a vegetable stall holding a cloth bag in one hand and a plastic bag in the other, with a thinking bubble above her.

agreed.text: We choose a material because its properties suit the job.
agreed.evidence: Engineers first write down what a job needs, such as 'strong', 'light' or 'waterproof'. Then they look up which materials have those properties, using big charts of materials.

agreed.text: Rubber grips most hard, dry surfaces better than paper, cloth or hard plastic.
agreed.evidence: In tilt tests like yours, things stay on rubber at a much steeper slope. This is why tyres, chappal soles and the feet of a mixie are made of rubber.

agreed.text: Friction happens wherever two surfaces touch and press together.
agreed.evidence: Even a polished steel katori on smooth glass needs a little tilt before it slides. With no friction at all, it would slide at the smallest tilt.

challenging.claim: A heavier katori will stay on a steeper tilt than a light one.
challenging.for: Heavy things are harder to push across the floor. A heavy katori presses down harder, so it grips more.
challenging.against: A heavier katori does grip more. But it is also pulled down the slope more, by the same amount. The two balance out. So on paper or cloth, a heavy and a light katori slide at about the same tilt. Leonardo da Vinci noticed this in his notebooks over 500 years ago. Guillaume Amontons in France showed it again in 1699.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make about the tilt test. You can test it yourself in the activity 'Heavy or Light'.

challenging.claim: The strongest material is always the best choice.
challenging.for: Strong things last long and do not break. Steel is used for bridges and buses.
challenging.against: A raincoat made of steel would be strong, but it could not bend and would be far too heavy. A towel made of steel could not soak up water. The best material is the one with the properties this job needs.
challenging.context: This card is about whether one material can be best for everything.

challenging.claim: Plastic is always the wrong material.
challenging.who: Some people who care about the Earth
challenging.for: Plastic litter blocks drains and harms cows, turtles, birds and other animals. Much plastic is used once and thrown away.
challenging.against: Plastic is light, waterproof and cheap. It keeps medicines clean and makes pipes that carry water to homes. Many people say the problem is plastic used once and thrown away, not every use of plastic.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument. Careful people disagree about it.

big_questions.q: Why did the katori stay on the rubber, when it slid off the plastic?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tiny bumps on the katori. Which material can squash into them?

big_questions.q: Can one property be good for one job and bad for another?
big_questions.hint: Think of rubber on a tray and rubber on a slide.

big_questions.q: Does a heavier katori grip better than a light one?
big_questions.hint: Test it. Put coins in the katori and try the same material again.

big_questions.q: If nothing in the world had any grip, what would happen at dinner time?
big_questions.hint: Think of plates, tumblers, your chair and your feet.

big_questions.q: Who decides what a material is for?
big_questions.hint: Patsy Sherman's mixture was made for one job and turned out right for another.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1953, Patsy Sherman was a young chemist at the 3M company in the USA. She and another chemist, Sam Smith, were trying to make a new kind of rubber for the fuel pipes of jet planes. One day, a lab assistant named Joan Mullan dropped a bottle of their test mixture. Drops splashed onto her canvas tennis shoe. Nothing would wash the spots off: not soap, not water, not the strongest cleaners. Most people would have called it a failed mixture and a spoiled shoe. But Sherman noticed something. As time went by, the splashed spots stayed clean, while the rest of the shoe got dirty. Water and oil ran off the spots. The mixture was wrong for a fuel pipe, but right for keeping cloth clean. Sherman and Smith worked on it for years. From 1956 it was sold as a stain guard for cloth, called Scotchgard. In 2000, the company said it would stop using one chemical in the old recipe, because that chemical stays in rivers and in bodies for a very long time. Choosing a material also means asking what happens to it afterwards.
how_we_found_out.who: Patsy Sherman and Sam Smith, chemists at the 3M company in the USA, and Joan Mullan, the lab assistant whose shoe was splashed
how_we_found_out.when: 1953; sold from 1956; the old recipe was stopped from 2000
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a mixture which failed at its job was useless. The splashed shoe showed it was the wrong material for a fuel pipe and the right one for keeping cloth clean.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman chemist in a 1950s lab looking closely at a canvas tennis shoe with one clean, bright spot on a dirty toe, while water drops roll off the spot.

story.title: The Tray That Would Not Sit Still
story.note: Buttermilk in steel tumblers is served in many South Indian homes. Many mixer grinders have rubber feet, and some families put a rubber mat under them to stop them moving. Kavya, Arjun, Amma and Paati are made up.
text: Kavya was eight. She lived with her Amma, her Paati and her little brother Arjun on the fourth floor of a building in Madurai.
It was Pongal, and the flat was full of guests. Paati poured cold buttermilk into six steel tumblers.
'Arjun, take the buttermilk to the guests,' said Amma. She put all six tumblers on a big steel tray.

Arjun was five. He held the tray with both hands and walked very slowly. But at the kitchen door, he tipped the tray a little. All six tumblers slid to one side with a loud clatter. Buttermilk splashed onto the floor.
'The tray is too slippery,' said Arjun. His lip shook.

Kavya helped him wipe the floor. Then she looked at the tray. It was smooth, shiny steel. The tumblers were smooth, shiny steel too. 'Steel on steel slides,' she said. 'We need something on the tray that grips.'
She tried a plastic sheet first, the kind that covers new books. She put a tumbler on it and tipped the tray a little. The tumbler slid off even faster.
'Worse,' said Arjun.
She tried a sheet of newspaper. The tumbler slid a little later, but it still slid.
She tried a cotton hanky. That was a little better again.
Then Kavya remembered the mixie. When Amma ground idli batter, the mixie used to shake and walk across the counter. So Amma had put a small rubber mat under it, and now it stayed still.

Kavya fetched the rubber mat and laid it on the tray. She put a tumbler on it. She tipped the tray, more and more. The tumbler stayed. She tipped it so far that Arjun gasped. Still the tumbler stayed.
'Rubber!' said Kavya. 'Rubber is the best material.'
Arjun carried the buttermilk again, on the rubber mat. Not one tumbler moved. The guests clapped, and Arjun grinned.
The next morning, the two of them went down to the play area of their building. There was a long steel slide, shiny from years of children sliding down it.
Arjun did not want to get his new shorts dirty. So he took the rubber mat with him and sat on it at the top of the slide.
He pushed off. He moved a tiny bit, and then he stopped, halfway down. He wriggled. He did not move. He was stuck on the slide, sitting on the rubber mat.
Kavya laughed so much that she had to sit down. Then she stopped laughing and thought.
'Yesterday rubber was the best,' she said. 'Today rubber is the worst.'
'Why?' asked Arjun, still stuck.
'The rubber did the same thing both times,' said Kavya slowly. 'It gripped. On the tray, we wanted grip. On the slide, you want to slip.'
She pulled the mat out from under him. Arjun shot down the shiny steel and landed on his feet, laughing.
At home, Kavya told Paati about the slide. Paati smiled and put down her glass.
'A spoon is good for rasam and bad for cutting vegetables,' Paati said. 'A knife is good for cutting and bad for rasam. You don't ask which one is good. You ask: good for what?'

That night, Kavya made a list on the back of a calendar page. On one side she wrote 'Needs grip': the tray, the mixie, chappals, the bathroom mat. On the other side she wrote 'Needs slip': the slide, the drawer in the kitchen, the carrom board.
Arjun drew a picture beside it. It showed a boy stuck halfway down a slide, on a rubber mat, with a very surprised face.
story.epiphany: A material is not good or bad on its own. The rubber gripped both times. That grip was right for the tray and wrong for the slide.
ask: Why did the tumblers slide off the steel tray?
What did the rubber do on the tray, and what did it do on the slide?
What did Paati mean by 'good for what?'
art: A small boy at a kitchen door with a steel tray tipping, and six steel tumblers of buttermilk sliding to one side.
A girl laughing at the bottom of a shiny steel slide in a building's play area, while her little brother sits stuck halfway down on a small rubber mat.

experiments.title: The Tilt Test: which material makes the best tray mat?
experiments.context: In this experiment you cover a board with rubber, cloth, newspaper, plastic or nothing. You put a steel katori on it and lift one end slowly. You measure how high the end is when the katori starts to slide.
experiments.question: Which material holds a steel katori on the steepest tilt? Which one lets it slide first?
experiments.predict: Feel each material with your fingers. Which one will hold the katori on the steepest tilt? Which one will let it slide first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same katori, with the same 10 coins in it, every time. We use the same board and lift the same end, slowly. We put the katori in the same place, in the middle. Only the material on the board changes. We try each material 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Good for a tray mat? Good for a slide?

materials.item: a flat wooden or plastic chopping board, or a big hardback book, about 30 cm long
10 coins, to put inside the katori
6 ordinary rubber bands, or a balloon cut open and laid flat
a cotton hanky or a piece of old cotton cloth, as big as the board
a plastic sheet: a clear book cover, a plastic file folder or a flat plastic bag

schedule.what: Feel and guess. Test each of the five surfaces 3 times. Write the heights. Choose a material for a tray mat and one for a slide.

experiments.record: Write your guess and your reason at the top. Fill in the results table. Circle the best material for a tray mat in green, and the best for a slide in blue.

setup.art: A wooden chopping board with six rubber bands stretched round it side by side, and a steel katori holding ten coins sitting in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Cover the board with one material. Put the katori on it.

setup.art: A child's hand slowly lifting one end of the chopping board while the other end rests on the floor, with a ruler held upright beside the lifted end.
setup.caption: 2. Lift one end slowly. Hold a ruler beside it.

setup.art: The katori starting to slide down the tilted board, and a finger pointing at the number on the ruler.
setup.caption: 3. When the katori slides, read the height.

setup.art: Five chopping boards in a row, covered with rubber bands, cloth, newspaper, a plastic sheet and nothing, each with a number written below.
setup.caption: 4. Do the same for each material. Compare.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the five surfaces: rubber bands, cloth, newspaper, plastic and the bare board. 2. Let your child rub each one with a finger. 3. Ask the question below. 4. Write down their guess and reason, word for word.
flow.say: Feel each one. Which will hold the katori on the steepest tilt? Which will let it slide first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Feel each one. Which will hold the katori best? Which will let it slide first? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will hold best?
good: The rubber, because it feels sticky.
The cloth, because it is rough.
The plastic will slide first, because it is smooth.

flow.parent: Don't say if the guess is right. Any guess with a reason is good. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tilt test. You feel five surfaces and guess which one grips a katori best.

flow.do: 1. Stretch 6 rubber bands round the board, side by side and close together. 2. Put 10 coins in the katori. 3. Put the katori in the middle of the board, on the bands. 4. Rest one end of the board on the floor.
flow.say: We put coins in the katori so it sits firmly. We use the same katori and the same coins every time.
flow.kid: Put the rubber bands round the board. Put 10 coins in the katori. Set it in the middle.
flow.parent: If the rubber bands are too small for the board, cut open a balloon, lay it flat and tape its edges down. Keep the bands flat and close together, so the katori sits on rubber, not on the gaps.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler upright on the floor, beside the end you will lift. 2. Lift that end very slowly, about as fast as a snail. 3. Stop the moment the katori starts to slide. 4. Read the height on the ruler. 5. Write it down. 6. Do it twice more.
flow.say: Lift it slowly, slowly. Watch the katori. Say 'Stop!' the moment it moves. How high is the end now?
flow.kid: Lift the end very slowly. Shout 'Stop!' when the katori moves. Read the ruler.

ask.q: How high did the end go before the katori slid?
good: About 20 cm.
Very high. It nearly tipped over before it slid.

flow.parent: A jerk makes the katori slide early, so lift smoothly. You can lift while your child reads the ruler, or the other way round. If the katori tips over instead of sliding, write 'tipped' and the height. That still means the rubber held it.

flow.do: 1. Take the rubber bands off. 2. Tape the cloth flat on the board. 3. Do three tries and write the heights. 4. Do the same with the newspaper, the plastic sheet and the bare board.
flow.say: Now we change only the material. Everything else stays the same. Which one do you think will be next?
flow.kid: Change the material. Keep the katori and coins the same. Test each one three times.
flow.parent: Tape the materials at the edges, under the board if you can, so the tape is not under the katori. The heights for cloth, newspaper and the bare board may be close together. That is a real result. Rubber usually holds the katori far higher than all the others.

flow.do: 1. For each material, circle the middle number of the three tries. 2. Ask your child to point to the highest and the lowest.
flow.say: Look at the middle numbers. Which material held the katori on the steepest tilt? Which let it slide first?
flow.kid: Find the biggest number and the smallest number. Which materials are they?

good: Yes, the rubber held it highest.
No, I thought the cloth would be best, but the rubber was best.

check.q: In your results table, what does a bigger number mean?
options: The material held the katori longer, so it grips more
check.why: The number is the height of the board when the katori slid. A bigger height means the katori stayed on longer. If your rubber number is small, check that the katori sat on the rubber and not on the tape.

flow.do: 1. Ask the first question below. 2. Then ask the second one. 3. Let your child answer both from the table.
flow.say: Paati wants a mat for her tray, so the tumblers don't slide. Which material should she use? Now a park needs a new slide. Which material should it be covered with?
flow.kid: Which material is best for a tray mat? Which is best for a slide? Look at your table.

ask.q: Why is the best tray material not the best slide material?
good: The tray needs grip and the slide needs slip.
Rubber grips, so you would get stuck on a rubber slide.

flow.parent: This is the main idea of the unit. The same result, rubber gripping, makes rubber the best for one job and the worst for the other. Let your child say it in their own words before you add anything.

activities.title: Does the Job Need It? Cross out what doesn't matter
activities.context: In this activity you look at four things in your home. You list the properties of each one's material, and cross out the properties its job does not need.

materials.item: a steel tumbler, an umbrella, a rubber chappal and a cotton towel

schedule.what: List the properties of four things. Cross out the ones each job does not need.

activities.record: For each thing, write its job, its material and its properties. Cross out the properties that do not help the job.

setup.art: A steel tumbler, a folded umbrella, a rubber chappal and a cotton towel in a row on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Put four things on the table.

setup.art: A page with 'tumbler: steel: holds water, does not break, shiny' and the word 'shiny' crossed out.
setup.caption: 2. List the properties. Cross out what the job doesn't need.

flow.do: 1. Pick up the steel tumbler. 2. Ask your child what job it does. 3. Ask them to name as many properties of steel as they can. 4. Write them all down.
flow.say: What is the tumbler's job? Now tell me everything steel is like. Hard? Shiny? Cold? Heavy?
flow.kid: What is the tumbler for? Say everything steel is like.

good: Hard, shiny, cold, heavy, does not break, waterproof.

flow.parent: Write every property they say, even ones that do not matter. Crossing out comes next.

flow.do: 1. Read the list back. 2. For each property, ask: 'Does the tumbler need this to do its job?' 3. Cross out each one it does not need.
flow.say: Does a tumbler need to be shiny to hold water? No. So we cross out shiny. Does it need to be waterproof?
flow.kid: Read each word. Does the tumbler need it? If not, cross it out.

good: Waterproof and does not break.
Hard, so it keeps its shape.

flow.parent: Shiny and cold are usually crossed out. A strong answer explains each choice: 'It needs to be waterproof, or the water would leak.'

flow.do: Do the same for the umbrella, the chappal and the towel. Let your child do as much as they can alone.
flow.say: Now the umbrella cloth. What does it need to be? What could we cross out?
flow.kid: Now do the umbrella, the chappal and the towel.
flow.parent: Umbrella cloth: waterproof and flexible matter, colour does not. Chappal: grippy and bendy matter. Towel: absorbent and soft matter. There is often more than one good answer.

check.q: Which property does a towel need for its job?
check.why: A towel's job is to dry you, so it must soak up water. A waterproof towel would leave you wet.

activities.title: The Grip and Slip Hunt
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find things that are made to grip, and things that are made to slip.

materials.item: paper, a green colour and a blue colour

schedule.what: Find 5 things made to grip and 3 made to slip. Draw them.

activities.record: Draw the grip things in green and the slip things in blue. Write the material under each one.

setup.art: A child turning over a mixie to look at the rubber feet underneath.
setup.caption: 1. Look for things made to grip.

setup.art: A child sliding a kitchen drawer open and closed.
setup.caption: 2. Look for things made to slip.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home with your child. 2. Look under the mixie, at chappal soles, the bathroom mat, bottle lids and bicycle handles. 3. Ask what each one is made of.
flow.say: Let's find things that are made to grip. Look under the mixie. Look at your chappal. What material is it?
flow.kid: Find 5 things that grip. Look under the mixie and at your chappal.

ask.q: What is the grippy part made of?
good: Rubber.
Rough plastic with little bumps.

flow.parent: Good grip things: chappal soles, the feet of a mixie, a bathroom mat, the ridges on a bottle lid, a bicycle handle, a rough doormat. Many are rubber.

flow.do: 1. Now look for things that need to slip. 2. Try a drawer, the carrom board, an iron box's flat bottom, a plastic comb through hair. 3. Draw all the things.
flow.say: Now find things that are meant to slide. What would happen if a drawer had a rubber bottom?
flow.kid: Find 3 things that slip. Draw all your things.
flow.parent: Do not test slipperiness by walking on wet floors. Looking and sliding things with your hands is enough. Look at the iron box only when it is unplugged and cool.

activities.title: Heavy or Light: does a heavier katori grip better?
activities.context: In this activity you test a guess many people make: that a heavier katori will stay on a steeper tilt than a light one.

materials.item: the board from the tilt test, covered with newspaper

schedule.what: Test the empty katori and the katori with 20 coins, 3 times each.

activities.record: Write the three heights for the empty katori and for the heavy one. Circle the middle numbers.

setup.art: An empty steel katori on a newspaper-covered board, next to the same katori full of coins.
setup.caption: 1. One empty katori. One with 20 coins.

setup.art: A child lifting the board slowly with a ruler beside it, as the heavy katori starts to slide.
setup.caption: 2. Lift slowly. Read the height when it slides.

flow.do: Ask the question below, and write down your child's guess and reason.
flow.say: Which will stay on a steeper tilt: the empty katori or the full one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which will stay on longer: empty or full? Why?

good: The full one, because it is heavy and presses down more.
The empty one, because it is light.

flow.do: 1. Test the empty katori 3 times, lifting slowly. 2. Write the heights. 3. Put 20 coins in it. 4. Test it 3 times again.
flow.say: Same board, same newspaper, same lifting. Only the weight changes. Lift slowly.
flow.kid: Test the empty one 3 times. Add the coins. Test 3 times again.
flow.parent: On newspaper, the two usually slide at about the same height. A difference of 1 or 2 cm counts as the same. If you see a big difference, check that you lifted at the same speed.

flow.do: Compare the middle numbers. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Did the heavy katori stay on a steeper tilt? What does that tell us about the guess?
flow.kid: Were they about the same? Was the guess right?

good: They slid at about the same height, so heavier does not grip better on a slope.

flow.parent: The heavier katori presses down harder and grips more. But it is also pulled down the slope more. The two balance out.

activities.title: A Suit for a Superhero
activities.context: In this activity you design a suit for a superhero who rescues people on a rainy, slippery hillside. You choose a material for each part, by its job.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper and colours

schedule.what: Draw the superhero. Choose and label a material for each part of the suit.

activities.record: Draw the suit. Label each part with its material and the job it does.

setup.art: A girl superhero standing on a wet, muddy hillside in the rain, with empty labels pointing to her boots, gloves, cape and hood.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the superhero on a rainy hill.

setup.art: The same drawing with labels filled in: 'boots: rubber, grip', 'cape: plastic, waterproof', 'gloves: rubber, grip'.
setup.caption: 2. Label each part: material and job.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child about the superhero below. 2. Ask what she will need.
flow.say: Our superhero, Mazhai Rani, rescues people on wet, muddy hills in the rain. What will her boots need? Her gloves? Her cape?
flow.kid: Mazhai Rani rescues people on wet hills. What does her suit need?

good: Grip, so she doesn't slip on the mud.
Waterproof, so her feet stay dry.

flow.parent: 'Mazhai' means rain in Tamil and Malayalam. Let your child name her too, if they like.

flow.kid: Draw her suit. Write a material for each part. Say why.
flow.parent: Strong answers: rubber boots and gloves for grip, a plastic or umbrella-cloth cape to keep water out, a bright colour so people can see her. Ask: 'Would a slippery material be good anywhere on her suit?'

games.title: Grip or Slip?
games.context: This is a moving game. A job card is read out. Everyone stamps their feet if the job needs grip, or slides their hands together if it needs slip.

items.b: Grip. Rubber stops you slipping on the road.
Slip. Smooth steel or plastic lets you slide down.

items.f: A mat for a tray of tumblers
items.b: Grip. Rubber stops the tumblers sliding.
Grip. It stops wet feet slipping on the tiles.
Slip. It must slide open easily.
Grip. Rubber or foam stops your hands sliding.

items.f: The bottom of a sledge on snow in Kashmir
items.b: Slip. A smooth bottom glides over snow.
Grip. Rubber feet stop the mixie moving.
Grip. A rough rope is easier to hold.
Slip. Smooth wood and powder let the coins glide.

items.f: The bottom of an iron box
items.b: Slip. Smooth metal glides over the clothes.
Grip. Its sole stops the player slipping.

rules: Cut out the 12 cards. Put them face down in a pile.
One player is the caller. The caller turns over the top card and reads the front out loud.
Everyone else does the move at once. Stamp your feet for grip. Slide your hands past each other for slip.
The caller reads the back. Everyone who did the right move gets a point.
Take turns being the caller. The player with the most points when the pile is used up wins.

setup.art: A pile of small cards on the floor, with the top card showing 'A chappal sole'.
setup.caption: 1. Read the job card.

setup.art: Two children: one stamping her feet, the other sliding his hands past each other.
setup.caption: 2. Stamp for grip. Slide your hands for slip.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Show your child the two moves.
flow.say: If a job needs grip, stamp your feet. If it needs to slip, slide your hands past each other, like this.
flow.kid: Stamp for grip. Slide your hands for slip. Try both.

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. On the count of three, everyone does a move. 3. Read the back and give points. 4. Ask why after each card.
flow.say: A mat for a tray of tumblers. One, two, three, move! Why did you stamp?
flow.kid: Listen to the job. Stamp or slide. Then say why.

ask.q: Why does a carrom board need slip?
good: So the coins glide when you flick them.

flow.parent: Give a point for any move with a good reason, even if the back says otherwise. A tug-of-war rope needs grip for the hands.

flow.do: Ask the question below to finish.
flow.say: Was there a card where grip would be a problem?
flow.kid: Which job would go wrong with too much grip?

ask.q: Which job would go wrong with grip?
good: The slide. You would get stuck.
The drawer would not open.

games.title: Job Detective
games.context: This is a guessing game. One player picks a secret job card. The others ask questions about the properties the job needs, and guess the job and a good material.

printables.title: 10 secret job cards to cut out

Needs: soaks up water, flexible. Good material: cotton.
Needs: waterproof, flexible. Good material: plastic.
Needs: grip. Good material: rubber.
Needs: slippery, strong, rigid. Good material: steel or plastic.
Needs: waterproof, strong. Good material: plastic or steel.
Needs: waterproof, flexible, strong. Good material: nylon or polyester umbrella cloth.
Needs: grip, waterproof. Good material: rubber or rough plastic.
Needs: strong, flexible. Good material: canvas or nylon cloth.
Needs: strong, flexible. Good material: nylon or coir rope.

items: Does it need to be slippery?
Does it need to be waterproof?
Does it need to soak up water?

Does it need to be rigid?
Does it need to be strong?

rules: Cut out all the cards. Lay the 8 question cards face up. Put the job cards face down.
The detective-keeper takes a job card and looks at it secretly.
The other players take turns to pick a question card and ask it. The keeper answers 'yes' or 'no', using the back of the job card.
After 5 questions, the other players guess the job and name a good material.
A right job gets 1 point. A suitable material gets 1 more point. Then the next player is keeper.

setup.caption: 2. Ask questions. Guess the job and a material.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read the 8 question cards aloud with your child.
flow.say: These are our detective questions. Each one asks about a property a job might need.
flow.kid: Read the question cards. Each asks what a job needs.

flow.do: 1. You start as the keeper, to show how it works. 2. Answer each question from the back of your card. 3. Swap roles after each round.
flow.say: I have a secret job. Ask me a question card.
flow.kid: Ask a question. Listen to yes or no. Guess the job.

ask.q: A card says only 'Needs: grip'. Which job is it, and which material is good?
good: A tray mat. Rubber would be good.

flow.parent: Help your child use the answers together: 'It needs grip and it needs to be waterproof. What could that be?'

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which question helped you most? Why?
flow.kid: Which question helped you most?

good: 'Does it need to grip?' because only a few jobs need grip.

projects.title: The Grip Map of Our Home
projects.context: In this project you make a map of your home over three days. You mark the places that need grip and the places that need slip, and find one place that needs better grip.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, a pencil, a green colour and a blue colour

schedule.what: Draw a simple map of the rooms in your home.
Mark grip places in green and slip places in blue, with the material.
Find one place that gets slippery when it should grip. Draw a fix.

projects.record: The finished map, with green and blue marks, a material by each mark, and one fix drawn in a box.

setup.art: A child drawing a simple map of a flat: kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, hall and balcony as boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: draw the rooms.

setup.art: The map with green dots by the bathroom mat and the door, and blue dots by a drawer and the carrom board.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: green for grip, blue for slip.

setup.art: A small box on the map showing a rubber mat drawn on a wet bathroom floor.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: draw one fix.

flow.do: 1. Help your child draw each room as a box. 2. Label the rooms.
flow.say: Let's draw our home from above, like a bird looking down. Each room is a box.
flow.kid: Draw each room as a box. Write its name.

flow.do: 1. Walk round with the map. 2. Mark grip places green and slip places blue. 3. Write the material by each mark.
flow.say: Where in the kitchen do we need grip? Where do we need things to slide?
flow.kid: Put green where things must grip. Put blue where they must slip.
flow.parent: Use the things from the Grip and Slip Hunt if you did it.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child where someone could slip at home. 2. Draw a box on the map showing a fix, and the material.
flow.say: Where could someone slip in our home? What material could we put there to help?
flow.kid: Where could someone slip? Draw a fix. What material is it?
flow.wait: Do this on the third day.
flow.parent: The wet bathroom floor is the usual answer. A rubber or rough mat, or rough tiles, are good fixes. Look and talk about it. Do not test it by slipping.

challenges.title: The Slipperiest Slide for a Matchbox
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. In the tilt test you looked for grip. Now you do the opposite: you make a slide that a matchbox slides down at the smallest tilt.
challenges.problem: Cover a piece of card to make a slide. A matchbox with 2 coins inside must slide down by itself. Make it slide with the end of the card lifted as low as you can.
constraints: Use one piece of card from a box, about 30 cm long.
The matchbox must start still and slide down by itself, without a push.
materials: a piece of stiff card from a carton, about 30 cm long
an empty matchbox with 2 coins inside
a plastic sheet or bag, foil, newspaper, butter paper and an unlit candle
general: Cover the card with a smooth plastic sheet and tape it at the back.
Cover the card with foil, smoothed flat.
creative: Rub an unlit candle all over the card, so a thin layer of wax makes it slippery.
Rub the candle on the bottom of the matchbox too.
challenges.your_turn: Try your own cover. Measure the lowest height where the matchbox slides by itself. Then try to make it slide even lower.

setup.art: A piece of card covered with a plastic sheet, one end on the floor, with a matchbox at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Cover the card. Put the matchbox at the top.

setup.art: A child lifting the card slowly, with a ruler beside it, as the matchbox slides down.
setup.caption: 2. Lift slowly. Measure when it slides.

setup.art: A child rubbing an unlit candle on a piece of card.
setup.caption: 3. Try to make it more slippery.

flow.do: Read the challenge to your child. Ask which material from the tilt test they will start with.
flow.say: This time we want slip, not grip. Which material let the katori slide first in our tilt test?
flow.kid: This time you want slip. Which material slipped most in the tilt test?

ask.q: Which material will you try first?
good: The plastic, because the katori slid off it first.

flow.do: 1. Your child covers the card. 2. They lift one end slowly and measure the height when the matchbox slides. 3. They try other covers and compare.
flow.say: Lift slowly. When does the matchbox start to slide? Can you make it slide lower?
flow.kid: Cover the card. Lift slowly. Measure. Try another cover.
flow.parent: Waxed card is usually very slippery. Keep the candle unlit. Lifting smoothly matters more than anything else.

flow.do: Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which cover made the best slide? Would it make a good tray mat?
flow.kid: Which cover was best for the slide? Would it be good on a tray?

ask.q: Would your slide cover make a good tray mat?
good: No. The tumblers would slide off it.

worksheets.title: Grip, Slip and the Right Material (core)

items.p: Draw a line from each job to the property it needs most.
items.why: Each job needs a different property. We choose the material by what the job needs.

items.p: In the tilt test, what do we measure?
opts: How high the lifted end is when the katori slides
items.why: We read the height of the lifted end at the moment the katori starts to slide. A bigger height means more grip.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: Friction is the grip between two things that touch.
items.why: True. Friction stops things sliding. It is why your chappal does not slip on the road.

items.p: Draw the tilted board with the katori sitting on the rubber bands. Draw an arrow to show which way the katori would slide.
items.a: A board with one end lifted, the katori on it, and an arrow pointing down the slope.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lifted end and an arrow pointing downhill. Things slide down a slope, not up.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.
items.art: An empty box to draw in.

items.p: Sort these jobs into 'needs grip' and 'needs slip'.
items.why: Things we hold or stand on need grip. Things that must move smoothly need slip.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why are chappal soles made of rubber?
items.a: Rubber grips the road, so you don't slip. It also bends when you walk.
items.why: A strong answer names the property, grip, and says why the job needs it.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2, is choosing a material for a new slide in her park. Which property does the slide need?
items.why: A slide must let children slide down. A grippy material, like a rubber mat, would make them stop halfway.

items.p: The grip between two things that touch is called ____.
items.why: Friction is the real word for grip between surfaces.

items.p: Nandini and her brother Farhan are making a mat for Paati's tea tray.

views.says: Use rubber. In our tilt test it held the katori on the steepest tilt.
Use cotton cloth. It soaks up spilt tea, and we can wash it.

items.ask: Whose choice would you pick? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason from the test, such as 'rubber held the katori highest'. It also says what the other is right about, such as 'cloth soaks up spills'.
items.why: Both are partly right. The best choice depends on which matters more: stopping slides or soaking up spills.

items.p: Ishita, a girl in Class 2, tested 5 materials in the tilt test. The katori slid off 4 of them before the board was 15 cm high. How many held the katori past 15 cm?
items.why: 5 materials take away 4 is 1. In most homes, that one is the rubber.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: Kavitha says, 'Steel is good for a tumbler because it is shiny.' What does a tumbler really need?
opts: To hold water and not break when dropped
items.why: Shiny does not help a tumbler hold water. Kavitha has named a property, but not one the job needs.

items.p: The steps of a city bus get wet in the rain. People must not slip on them. What material would you put on the steps, and why?
items.a: Rubber, or rough metal with ridges, because it grips wet shoes.
items.why: A strong answer says the job needs grip, even when wet, and names a grippy material.

items.p: Three of these are made to grip. Which one is made to slip?
items.why: The slide is made smooth so you can slide down. The other three are made to grip.

items.p: These are made-up results from a tilt test: rubber 20 cm, plastic 6 cm, newspaper 10 cm. Put them in order, from the one that let the katori slide first to the one that held it longest.
items.why: The smallest height means the katori slid first. The biggest height means it held on longest.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: A katori full of coins always stays on a steeper tilt than an empty katori.
items.why: False. The full katori presses down harder and grips more, but it is also pulled down the slope more. On paper or cloth, they slide at about the same tilt.

items.p: A park in Hyderabad needs a new slide. Revathi and Gurpreet disagree.

views.says: Make it of steel. Steel is very slippery and lasts for years in the rain.
Make it of plastic. A steel slide gets burning hot in the summer sun, and plastic hurts less.

items.ask: Which would you choose? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason, such as 'plastic is not as hot to touch'. It also gives the other side its due, such as 'steel lasts longer'.
items.why: Both are real reasons. A slide has more than one job: to be slippery, to last, and to be safe to touch in the sun.

items.p: Draw a silly tray mat made of a very slippery material. Show what happens to the tumblers.
items.a: A tray with a shiny plastic mat and tumblers sliding off.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tumblers sliding, because a slippery mat has little grip.

items.p: Label each part of the umbrella with its material and the job it does.
a: the cover: umbrella cloth, keeps rain out and folds up
the thin ribs: metal, strong and thin
the handle: plastic or wood, easy to hold
items.why: One thing can use several materials. Each part's material suits that part's job.
items.art: An open umbrella with three empty labels pointing to the cover, a rib and the handle.

items.p: In the tilt test, why do we lift the board very slowly?
opts: So a jerk does not make the katori slide too early
items.why: A sudden jerk can start the katori sliding before the tilt is high enough. Lifting slowly makes the test fair.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: A material that is right for a job is called ____ for that job.
items.why: Suitable means it has the properties the job needs.

items.p: Meenakshi and her cousin Anitha are arguing about rubber.

views.says: Rubber is a good material. It held the katori best in our tilt test.
Rubber is a bad material. It made me stick halfway down the slide.

items.ask: Who is right? Give a reason. Then say what the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer says both are right about different jobs: rubber's grip is good for a tray and bad for a slide.
items.why: Grip is not good or bad on its own. It is good or bad for a job.

items.p: A mixture was made for one job, but it turned out to be right for a different one. Water and oil run straight off it. What everyday job could it be right for, and what property makes it right?
items.a: Keeping cloth clean, as a stain guard. Water and oil run off it, so spills and dirt do not soak in.
items.why: A strong answer names the new job and the property that made the material suit it.

items.p: Sindhu, a girl in Class 2, ran the tilt test once. The katori slid off the cloth at 12 cm. Her brother tried it and got 9 cm. What should they do?
opts: Try it 3 more times and look at the middle number
items.why: One try can be a fluke. More tries show what usually happens.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: Design a tray for a tea seller who carries tumblers of tea through a moving train. Label the material on top and say why you chose it.
items.a: A tray with a rubber mat, or holes for each tumbler, labelled with the material and the reason.
items.why: A strong design gives grip, or holds each tumbler in place, because the train shakes and tips.
items.art: An empty box to draw in, with lines for labels.

items.p: A ramp at the entrance of a building helps people in wheelchairs and people with walking sticks. Which surface is most suitable?
opts: Rough, so it grips wheels and feet
items.why: A ramp is a slope. Without grip, wheels and feet slide back down, like the katori on the plastic.

items.p: Sort each job by the property it needs most.
items.why: Every job has its own needs. The same material can be right for one and wrong for another.

items.p: If a material fails at one job, it is useless.
items.why: False. Patsy Sherman's mixture failed as a fuel pipe rubber and became a stain guard for cloth. Rubber fails as a slide and works as a tray mat.

items.p: Rubber is soft and squashes into tiny bumps. Use this to explain why the katori held on to rubber longer than to the hard plastic.
items.a: The rubber squashed into the tiny bumps under the katori and touched it in many places. The hard plastic touched it in only a few places, so there was less grip.
items.why: A strong answer links 'soft' to 'touches in more places' to 'more grip'.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: Gauri's katori stayed on the rubber until 20 cm. It slid off the plastic at 5 cm. Count in 5s from 5 to 20. How many 5s is that?
items.why: 5, 10, 15, 20 is four 5s. So the rubber held the katori 4 times as high as the plastic.
items.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.

items.p: Label each part of the pressure cooker with its material and its job.
a: the body: steel or aluminium, strong and carries heat to the food
the ring inside the lid: rubber, bends to seal the steam in
the handle: hard plastic, does not get very hot, so you can hold it
items.why: A pressure cooker uses three materials, each suited to its own part of the job.
items.art: A pressure cooker with its lid on, and three empty labels pointing to the body, the rubber ring and the handle.

videos.why: Shows how the job decides which material is suitable.
videos.check: Found by search: "Materials And Their Properties" by ClickView, 4 minutes. A parent may preview it.

opts: The grip between two things that touch
quiz.why: Friction is grip between surfaces. Picking 'a kind of rubber' mixes up the grip with one material that grips well.

quiz.p: Hema, a girl in Class 2, puts a katori on rubber bands and then on a plastic sheet, and tilts the board. Which holds the katori on a steeper tilt?
quiz.why: Rubber grips much better. Picking 'both the same' may mean thinking only the katori matters, not what it sits on.

quiz.p: Which job needs a slippery material?
quiz.why: A slide must let you slide down. Chappals and bathroom mats must stop you slipping.

quiz.p: Why is rubber a poor material to cover a slide?
opts: It grips, so you would stop halfway
quiz.why: Rubber's grip is the very thing that makes it a good tray mat and a bad slide.

quiz.p: Revathi's tumbler is steel. Which property matters most for a tumbler's job?
opts: It holds water and does not break when dropped
quiz.why: A tumbler must hold drinks and survive a fall. Shiny and cold do not help the job.

quiz.p: In the tilt test, why do we use the same katori and the same coins for every material?
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Then we know the material made the difference.

quiz.p: Paati wants her tea tumblers to stay still on a tray. Which mat is most suitable?
quiz.why: Rubber grips. Foil and a plastic sheet are smooth, so the tumblers slide.

quiz.p: Lalitha thinks cloth will grip better than newspaper. What should she do next?
opts: Test both on the tilted board and compare
quiz.why: A guess becomes something we know only after a test.

quiz.p: A new material makes water and oil run straight off it, instead of soaking in. Which job would it be right for?
quiz.why: If water and oil run off, spills cannot soak into cloth, so it works as a stain guard. A material wrong for one job can be right for another.

quiz.p: A raincoat must keep water out and bend when you move. Which material is suitable?
quiz.why: Plastic is waterproof and flexible. Steel is waterproof but rigid. Newspaper soaks up water.

quiz.p: Why does soft rubber grip a katori so well?
opts: It squashes into the tiny bumps and touches in many places
quiz.why: More places touching means more grip. Picking 'it is wet' may come from wet floors, but water usually makes things slip.

applications: Tyres, chappal soles and shoe soles are made of rubber, for grip on the road.
Slides, drawer runners and the bottom of an iron box are made smooth, so things slip.
Bathroom mats and rough tiles help stop people slipping on wet floors.
Ramps for wheelchairs are given a rough surface, so wheels and feet grip.
Engineers choose materials for bridges, buses and phones by listing what each part's job needs.

spotted.text: A coir doormat at the door of a flat. Coir, from coconut husk, is rough, so it scrapes mud off shoes and does not slide. Much of India's coir is made in Kerala.

spotted.text: The rubber feet under a mixie, so it stays put while it grinds idli batter or chutney.

spotted.text: Carrom powder sprinkled on a carrom board in a Kolkata or Chennai home, so the coins glide.
spotted.art: A hand sprinkling white powder on a carrom board, with coins and a striker.

spotted.text: A shiny steel slide in a park in Pune, worn smooth by children sliding down it.
spotted.art: Children queueing at the top of a shiny steel slide in a park.

spotted.text: The rubber ring inside a pressure cooker lid. It bends to seal the steam in.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does friction work, down at the level of the tiniest particles?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure friction very well. But explaining it from the tiny particles where two surfaces touch is still hard, and scientists still study and argue about it.

open_questions.q: Can we make a material that grips when we want, and slips when we want?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are making materials that can switch their grip, some copying the toes of geckos. A few work in labs, but none is in every home yet.

ask_kids: Which of your chappals grips the floor best? Why do you think so?
What would happen if a slide were covered with rubber?
Where in our home could someone slip? What material could help?
Why do you think a carrom board is so smooth?
If you could invent a new material, what job would it do?

jokes.j: Why did the katori love the rubber mat?
What did the slide say to the rubber mat?
Why was the drawer so happy?
What did the chappal say to the wet road?
jokes.a: I've got a grip on this!

jokes.j: Why did the tumbler slide off the steel tray?
jokes.a: It had nothing to hold on to.

jokes.j: What is a carrom coin's favourite way to travel?
Why did the paper umbrella go home early?
jokes.a: It couldn't handle the pressure of the rain!

jokes.j: What did the towel say to the raincoat?
Why did Arjun stop halfway down the slide?
jokes.a: He was sitting on too much friction!

maths.problem: In the tilt test, the katori slid off the plastic sheet at 6 cm. It stayed on the rubber until 20 cm. How many centimetres higher did the rubber hold it?
maths.explain: Count on from 6 to 20. From 6 to 10 is 4. From 10 to 20 is 10. 4 and 10 make 14. So the rubber held the katori 14 cm higher.
maths.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.
maths.why_maths: Taking one height from the other tells us how much better the rubber gripped.

maths.problem: Made-up results: cloth 12 cm, newspaper 10 cm, bare board 9 cm, plastic 6 cm, rubber 20 cm. Put them in order from the most grip to the least. Which two are closest together?
maths.answer: Rubber 20, cloth 12, newspaper 10, bare board 9, plastic 6. Newspaper and the bare board are closest: only 1 cm apart.
maths.explain: The biggest height means the most grip. 10 and 9 differ by 1, which is the smallest gap. With such a small gap, one more try might swap them.
maths.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.
maths.why_maths: Putting the heights in order shows which material grips best, and close numbers tell us when we cannot be sure.

maths.problem: Ishita tried the rubber 3 times. The katori slid at 20 cm, 23 cm and 21 cm. Put the three numbers in order. Which one is in the middle?
maths.explain: In order, the numbers are 20, 21 and 23. The middle one is 21. We use the middle number because one strange try, too high or too low, does not change it much.
maths.context: This question is about the tilt test. You put a steel katori on a board covered with different materials, lift one end slowly, and measure how high it is when the katori slides.
maths.why_maths: Three tries give three slightly different numbers. The middle one is a fair number to write down.

maths.problem: In the Grip and Slip Hunt, Tejal found 7 things made to grip and 3 things made to slip. Draw one green circle for each grip thing and one blue circle for each slip thing. How many more grip things did she find?
maths.explain: 7 green circles and 3 blue circles. Match them in pairs: 3 pairs, and 4 green circles are left over. So 7 take away 3 is 4.
maths.context: This question is about the Grip and Slip Hunt, where you walk round your home and find things made to grip and things made to slip.
maths.why_maths: A picture with one circle for each thing shows at a glance which group is bigger, and by how much.

warmup.a: The grip between two things that touch.

warmup.q: Name one thing made to grip.
warmup.a: A chappal sole, a bathroom mat, a bicycle handle or the feet of a mixie.

warmup.q: Name one thing made to slip.
warmup.a: A slide, a drawer or a carrom board.

warmup.q: Which material held the katori best in the tilt test?

warmup.a: Right for a job, because it has the properties the job needs.

warmup.q: Why is rubber bad for a slide?
warmup.a: It grips, so you would stop halfway.

roots.context: We have tested which material grips a katori, and used the results to choose a tray mat and a slide. Now we ask what the tilt test tells us about materials, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: On your tilted board, the soft rubber held the hard steel katori long after the others let go. The rubber squashed into tiny bumps under the katori and touched it in many more places. The hard, smooth plastic touched only the tops of those bumps. So a soft material can grip better than a hard one.
deep_truth.habit: We think hard materials hold things best, and that soft ones are weak. In the tilt test, soft rubber gave by far the best grip.
deep_truth.evidence: In the tilt test, the same katori with the same coins slid off the plastic at a low tilt and stayed on the rubber until the board was much higher. Rubber is soft enough to squash into the tiny bumps of a surface, so it touches in many more places. This is why tyres, chappal soles and the feet of a mixie are soft rubber.

three.who_am_i: You need grip too. Your bare feet grip a dry floor, and slip on a soapy one.
three.what_is_life: A house gecko walks across your ceiling. Tiny hairs on their toes give them the grip their life needs.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything that touches something else has some friction. With no grip at all, nothing in the world would stay where it was put.

roots.thread: Rubber and steel are made of tiny particles. Where they touch, the particles hold on to each other, and that holding is part of friction. Everything is conscious, so this holding is also a meeting, where each material answers the other. Many physicists describe it only as electric forces between particles, with no awareness in it. Either way, the job comes from someone who needs it: the same meeting helps on a tray and gets in the way on a slide.

teachings.teaching: Socrates says you could cut a vine branch with a dagger or a kitchen knife. But nothing cuts it as well as a pruning knife, made for that job.
teachings.link: Socrates says a tool is best when it is made for the job. You chose rubber for the tray mat in the same way.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 4 (In the World of Men), the carpenter and the oak at the shrine
teachings.teaching: A carpenter passed a huge oak and called the tree useless. Boats from their wood would sink, and doors would ooze sap. That night the oak spoke to him in a dream. Being useless to carpenters, the oak said, was what had let them grow so old and so great.
teachings.link: The oak's wood was wrong for the carpenter's jobs and right for the oak's own long life. Useful always means useful for someone's job.

science.text: Rubber grips well partly because it is soft. It squashes into the tiny bumps of the other surface and touches it in many more places.
Scientists still cannot fully explain friction from what the tiny particles do where two surfaces touch.

other_view.view: A material that is strong, lasts long and is cheap does well at almost every job, so it is fair to call it a good material.

practice.title: Grip and slip with your hands
practice.say: Press your palms together and slide them slowly past each other. Feel how they grip. Now put a hanky between them and slide again. Feel how they slip. Now sit very still. Feel the floor holding you up, and the chair holding you in place. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out. Everything you touch is gripping you a little, all the time.
practice.kid: Press your palms together. Slide them slowly. Feel the grip. Now put a hanky between them. Slide again. Sit still. Feel the floor holding you.

ask: If nothing had any grip, could anything stay where you put it?
Is a material good, or is it only good for something?
Who decides what a material's job is: the person, or the material?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with palms pressed together, with a steel tray holding still tumblers on one side and a shiny slide on the other.

founder: ideas/by_topic/materials-and-their-properties.md: the science journal pages 'SuperHero Suit Design' (p70 to p74), used for the activity 'A Suit for a Superhero'. The SCI cards there are used at other levels.

Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2, Unit 3 'Getting materials right' (sensible and silly materials, 'Why is that material useful?', and Sam's idea that a property the job does not need does not matter): used for the cross-out activity and the explanation 'start with the job'. The tilt test is new, so as not to repeat the Class 1 spoon and wrapper tests or the Class 3 heat tests.
science: Rubber friction: soft rubber deforms into surface roughness and adheres, giving high friction on hard surfaces (B. N. J. Persson, 'Theory of rubber friction and contact mechanics', Journal of Chemical Physics 115, 2001).

Amontons' laws of friction (G. Amontons, 1699): friction is proportional to load, so the angle at which a block slides does not depend on its weight. Leonardo da Vinci recorded similar findings in his notebooks around 1493 (I. M. Hutchings, 'Leonardo da Vinci's studies of friction', Wear 360, 2016).

Patsy Sherman and Samuel Smith, 3M, 1953: a fluorochemical rubber for jet fuel hoses spilt on a lab assistant's canvas shoe; the spot resisted water, oil and solvents and stayed clean. Sold as Scotchgard from 1956 (National Inventors Hall of Fame; Lemelson-MIT). 3M announced the phase-out of PFOS chemistry in May 2000.

Shopping bag life-cycle studies: a cotton bag must be reused many times to have lower impacts than a single-use plastic bag (UK Environment Agency, 'Life cycle assessment of supermarket carrier bags', 2011).
Gecko adhesion by foot hairs (setae): K. Autumn and others, 'Adhesive force of a single gecko foot-hair', Nature 405 (2000).
Plato, Republic 352e to 353a (the pruning knife and the function of each thing). Zhuangzi, chapter 4, the carpenter Shi and the oak tree at the earth shrine.
sources.walkthrough: Tilt test checked as a parent and child in a flat: a 30 cm chopping board, a steel katori with 10 coins, rubber bands stretched round the board, cloth, newspaper, a plastic sheet and the bare board, three slow lifts each, about 25 minutes.

playtest: New unit. The tilt test uses only a chopping board, a katori, coins, rubber bands, cloth, newspaper and a plastic sheet. Rubber gives a clearly higher tilt than the rest; the other materials may come out close together, and the steps say so.
